topic: Algebra III - Permutations & Combinations, Matrices & Determinants

sections.title: Circular Permutations
sections.content: Arranging 'n' distinct objects in a circle yields (n-1)! ways because there is no fixed starting point. If clockwise and anti-clockwise arrangements are identical (like flowers in a garland/necklace), it is (n-1)! / 2.

sections.title: Permutations with Repetition
sections.content: If you have 'n' objects where 'p' are of one type, 'q' of another, and 'r' of another, the total number of unique arrangements is n! / (p! * q! * r!).

sections.title: Properties of Determinants
sections.content: Important rules: 1) Swapping two rows/columns flips the determinant's sign. 2) If two rows/columns are identical, det = 0. 3) A scalar multiplied to a determinant multiplies only ONE row/column.

sections.title: Transpose, Symmetric & Skew-Symmetric Matrices
sections.content: Transpose (A^T) switches rows and columns. If A^T = A, it is symmetric. If A^T = -A, it is skew-symmetric (its diagonal elements must be 0). Any square matrix can be expressed as the sum of a symmetric and skew-symmetric matrix.

sections.title: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
sections.content: The adjoint (adj A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. The inverse of a matrix undoes it: A^-1 = (1/|A|) * adj(A). An inverse only exists if |A| ≠ 0 (non-singular matrix).

sections.title: Cramer's Rule (System of Equations)
sections.content: Used to solve linear equations using determinants. x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D, where D is the determinant of coefficients, and Dx is D with the x-column replaced by constant terms.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Dividing |kA| by k instead of k^n, where n is the matrix order.
2) Forgetting that (AB)^T = B^T A^T (Reverse order law).
3) Overcounting in circular permutations by not subtracting 1 from n.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 handles advanced counting (circles, repeated items) and essential matrix manipulations (properties, inverses, Cramer's rule) crucial for JEE problem-solving.

tricks.title: Bundle Method (Things Together)
tricks.explanation: If certain items must always be together (like vowels in a word), tie them in a "bundle" and treat them as 1 unit. Then multiply by the internal arrangement of the bundle.
tricks.example: Vowels together in 'EQUATION': (5 vowels bundle) + 3 consonants = 4 units. Total ways = 4! * 5! = 24 * 120.

tricks.title: Gap Method (Things Never Together)
tricks.explanation: If certain items must not sit together, arrange the other items first, creating 'gaps' between them. Then place the restricted items in those gaps.
tricks.example: Arrange 5 boys and 3 girls so no girls are together: Arrange boys (5!). They create 6 gaps. Place girls: 6P3. Total = 5! * 6P3.

tricks.title: Determinant Scalar Trick
tricks.explanation: When pulling a scalar 'k' out of a matrix determinant, it gets raised to the power of the matrix's order 'n'.
tricks.example: |kA| = k^n * |A|. If A is a 3x3 matrix, |2A| = 2³|A| = 8|A|.

tricks.title: Product of Determinants
tricks.explanation: The determinant of a product of matrices is the product of their individual determinants.

tricks.title: Quick Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
tricks.explanation: For [a b; c d], swap 'a' and 'd', change the signs of 'b' and 'c', and divide the whole matrix by its determinant (ad-bc).

tricks.title: Adjoint Determinant Trick
tricks.explanation: The determinant of an adjoint matrix can be found directly from the original determinant.
tricks.example: |adj A| = |A|^(n-1), where n is the order. For a 3x3 matrix, |adj A| = |A|².
